summary.text: Polynomials \(Q_k\) are constructed with \(Q_k'+Q_k=[x(1-x)]^k\), and their endpoint values are identified—via the shared recurrence—with signed factorial multiples of the odd-indexed numerator and denominator terms; the mean value theorem and \(0\le x(1-x)\le 1/4\) then give a factorial-exponential bound tending to zero for \(b_{2k+1}e-a_{2k+1}\). The recurrence expresses each even-indexed error as a linear combination of two neighboring odd-indexed errors, yielding an \(O(1/k)\) bound; since all eventual denominators are at least \(1\), dividing the vanishing errors by them proves the ratio limit.

full_proof.text:
Let \(e=\exp(1)\). We first work with integer-valued sequences \(A_n,B_n\), because the even part of the OEIS recurrence is naturally a subtraction in the integers. Define
\[
 A_0=0,\quad A_1=3,\quad A_2=5,
 \qquad
 B_0=0,\quad B_1=1,\quad B_2=2.
\]
For \(n\ge 3\), define both sequences by the same recurrence: if \(n\) is odd, then
\[
 X_n=2X_{n-1}+nX_{n-2},                                      \tag{1}
\]
and if \(n\) is even, then
\[
 X_n=\frac{n+2}{2}X_{n-1}-X_{n-2}-\frac{n-2}{2}X_{n-3}.       \tag{2}
\]
Here \(X\) may be either \(A\) or \(B\). Since the coefficients in (2) are integers when \(n\) is even, these are integer sequences.

We will prove
\[
 \frac{A_n}{B_n}\longrightarrow e.                            \tag{3}
\]
At the end we identify these integer sequences with the natural-number sequences in the question.

## 1. Useful consequences of the recurrence

Putting odd and even indices into (1) and (2), for either sequence \(X\) we get
\[
 X_{2k+3}=2X_{2k+2}+(2k+3)X_{2k+1},                           \tag{4}
\]
and
\[
 X_{2k+4}=(k+3)X_{2k+3}-X_{2k+2}-(k+1)X_{2k+1}.               \tag{5}
\]
Eliminate \(X_{2k+2}\) from (5) by means of (4). Multiplying (5) by \(2\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2X_{2k+4}
 &=2(k+3)X_{2k+3}-2X_{2k+2}-2(k+1)X_{2k+1}\\
 &=(2k+5)X_{2k+3}+X_{2k+1}.                                  \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying (4) at the next odd index and then using (6), we also obtain the two-step recurrence among odd-index terms
\[
 X_{2k+5}=(4k+10)X_{2k+3}+X_{2k+1}.                           \tag{7}
\]

We record positivity facts that will be needed later. For \(B\), direct calculation gives
\[
 B_1=1,\qquad B_3=2B_2+3B_1=7.
\]
Equation (7), whose coefficient \(4k+10\) is positive, proves inductively that every odd-index term \(B_{2k+1}\) is at least \(1\). Also \(B_2=2\), and (6) expresses twice every later even-index term as
\[
 2B_{2k+4}=(2k+5)B_{2k+3}+B_{2k+1}.
\]
The right side is positive (indeed at least \(2k+6\)), so, since \(B_{2k+4}\) is an integer, \(B_{2k+4}\ge1\). Thus
\[
 B_n\ge1\qquad(n\ge1).                                       \tag{8}
\]

The analogous argument gives nonnegativity of \(A\). Indeed,
\(A_1=3\) and \(A_3=2A_2+3A_1=19\). Equation (7) inductively makes all odd-indexed \(A_n\) nonnegative, and (6) then makes all even-indexed terms from index \(4\) onward nonnegative. Together with \(A_0=0,A_2=5\), this proves
\[
 A_n\ge0\qquad(n\ge0).                                       \tag{9}
\]

## 2. A family of polynomials

For \(k\ge0\), set
\[
 P_k(x)=x^k(1-x)^k.
\]
We construct real polynomials \(Q_k\) satisfying
\[
 Q_k'(x)+Q_k(x)=P_k(x).                                       \tag{10}
\]
Start with
\[
 Q_0(x)=1,
 \qquad
 Q_1(x)=-x^2+3x-3.
\]
These satisfy (10), since \(Q_0'+Q_0=1=P_0\), while
\[
 Q_1'+Q_1=(-2x+3)+(-x^2+3x-3)=x-x^2=P_1.
\]

For \(m\ge2\), introduce the correction polynomial
\[
 R_m(x)=-x^{m-1}(1-x)^{m-1} igl(x^2-(2m+1)x+m\bigr).          \tag{11}
\]
Define the remaining \(Q_m\)'s recursively by
\[
 Q_{k+2}
 =-(4(k+2)-2)(k+2)Q_{k+1}
  +(k+2)(k+1)Q_k+R_{k+2}.                                    \tag{12}
\]

We claim that (10) holds for every \(k\). Suppose it holds at indices \(k\) and \(k+1\). Differentiate (12) and add (12) itself. Substitution of the two induction hypotheses reduces the desired identity to
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{k+2}={}&-(4(k+2)-2)(k+2)P_{k+1}
 +(k+2)(k+1)P_k\\
&\quad+R_{k+2}'+R_{k+2}.                                     \tag{13}
\end{aligned}
\]
This is a direct polynomial identity. To check it, substitute
\(P_j=x^j(1-x)^j\) and (11), apply the product rule to \(R_{k+2}\), and factor out \(x^k(1-x)^k\). The remaining expression is a polynomial of degree at most four; collecting the powers of \(x\) gives exactly \(x^2(1-x)^2\), which is the remaining factor in \(P_{k+2}\). Thus (13) holds, and two-step induction proves (10) for all \(k\).

The correction term vanishes at both endpoints:
\[
 R_m(0)=R_m(1)=0\qquad(m\ge2),                                \tag{14}
\]
because it contains \(x^{m-1}(1-x)^{m-1}\). Evaluating (12) at either \(t=0\) or \(t=1\), therefore, gives
\[
 Q_{k+2}(t)=-(4(k+2)-2)(k+2)Q_{k+1}(t)
 +(k+2)(k+1)Q_k(t).                                          \tag{15}
\]

## 3. Endpoint values and the odd terms of the sequences

Define scaled versions of the odd terms by
\[
 a_k=(-1)^{k+1}(k+1)!A_{2k+1},
 \qquad
 b_k=(-1)^{k+1}(k+1)!B_{2k+1}.                               \tag{16}
\]
Using (7), together with
\((k+3)!=(k+3)(k+2)(k+1)!\) and the alternating sign in (16), one obtains
\[
 a_{k+2}=-(4(k+3)-2)(k+3)a_{k+1}+(k+3)(k+2)a_k,               \tag{17}
\]
and exactly the same recurrence for \(b_k\).

These are precisely the endpoint recurrences (15), shifted by one index. We now compare initial values. Since \(A_1=3,A_3=19\),
\[
 a_0=-3,\qquad a_1=2\cdot19=38.
\]
Also
\[
 Q_1(0)=-3.
\]
For \(Q_2\), formula (12) with \(k=0\), together with \(R_2(0)=0\), yields
\[
 Q_2(0)=-12Q_1(0)+2Q_0(0)=36+2=38.
\]
Thus (17) and (15) imply by two-step induction that
\[
 a_k=Q_{k+1}(0).                                              \tag{18}
\]

Similarly, \(B_1=1,B_3=7\), so
\[
 b_0=-1,\qquad b_1=14.
\]
Now \(Q_1(1)=-1\), and
\[
 Q_2(1)=-12Q_1(1)+2Q_0(1)=12+2=14.
\]
Consequently
\[
 b_k=Q_{k+1}(1).                                              \tag{19}
\]

## 4. Analytic bound for the odd-index errors

Fix \(m\ge0\), and consider
\[
 F_m(x)=Q_m(x)e^x.
\]
By (10),
\[
 F_m'(x)=(Q_m'(x)+Q_m(x))e^x=P_m(x)e^x.
\]
The mean value theorem on \([0,1]\) therefore supplies a point \(c\in(0,1)\) such that
\[
 Q_m(1)e-Q_m(0)=P_m(c)e^c.                                   \tag{20}
\]
For \(0<c<1\), one has
\[
 0\le c(1-c)\le\frac14,

the upper bound following, for example, from
\(c(1-c)=\frac14-(c-\frac12)^2\). Also \(e^c\le e\). Hence
\[
 0\le P_m(c)e^c=[c(1-c)]^m e^c\le\frac{e}{4^m}.              \tag{21}
\]

Apply (20)–(21) with \(m=k+1\), and use (18)–(19). We get
\[
 0\le b_ke-a_k\le\frac{e}{4^{k+1}}.                          \tag{22}
\]
On the other hand, definition (16) gives
\[
 b_ke-a_k
 =(-1)^{k+1}(k+1)!\bigl(B_{2k+1}e-A_{2k+1}\bigr).
\]
Taking absolute values in (22) therefore proves
\[
 \left|B_{2k+1}e-A_{2k+1}\right|
 \le \frac{e}{(k+1)!4^{k+1}}.                                \tag{23}
\]
In particular, the errors on the odd subsequence tend to zero.

## 5. Bounds for the even-index errors

Write
\[
 D_n=B_ne-A_n.
\]
Apply (6) once to \(A\) and once to \(B\), subtract, and divide by \(2\). This gives
\[
 D_{2k+4}=\frac{2k+5}{2}D_{2k+3}+\frac12D_{2k+1}.             \tag{24}
\]
Using the triangle inequality and (23) at indices \(2k+3\) and \(2k+1\), we find
\[
 |D_{2k+4}|
 \le e\left(
 \frac{(2k+5)/2}{(k+2)!4^{k+2}}
 +\frac{1/2}{(k+1)!4^{k+1}}
 \right).                                                    \tag{25}
\]

For completeness, the quantity in parentheses is at most \(4/(k+1)\). More generally, for every integer \(r\ge1\),
\[
 \frac{(2r+3)/2}{(r+1)!4^{r+1}}+
 \frac{1/2}{r!4^r}\le\frac4r.                               \tag{26}
\]
Indeed, \((r+1)!4^{r+1}\ge r^2\) and \(r!4^r\ge r\), so the left side is at most
\[
 \frac{2r+3}{2r^2}+\frac1{2r}=
 \frac{3r+3}{2r^2}\le\frac4r,
\]
where the last inequality is \(3\le5r\). Taking \(r=k+1\) in (26), equation (25) gives
\[
 |D_{2k+4}|\le\frac{4e}{k+1}.                                \tag{27}
\]
Thus the errors on the even subsequence also tend to zero; omitting the first two even indices clearly does not affect its limit.

Every natural number is either \(2k\) or \(2k+1\). Since both corresponding subsequences of \(D_n\) tend to zero, it follows directly from the \(\varepsilon\)-definition of convergence (take the larger of suitable even and odd thresholds) that
\[
 D_n=B_ne-A_n\longrightarrow0.                               \tag{28}
\]

## 6. Passage from errors to ratios

By (8), \(B_n\ge1\) for every \(n\ge1\). Hence
\[
 \left|\frac{D_n}{B_n}\right|\le |D_n|\qquad(n\ge1).
\]
Together with (28), the squeeze theorem yields
\[
 \frac{D_n}{B_n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
For \(n\ge1\), \(B_n\ne0\), and therefore
\[
 \frac{D_n}{B_n}
 =\frac{B_ne-A_n}{B_n}
 =e-\frac{A_n}{B_n}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \frac{A_n}{B_n}\longrightarrow e,                           \tag{29}
\]
as claimed.

## 7. Identification with the OEIS natural-number definitions

The sequences in the question are defined as natural numbers, with initial values
\[
\mathcal A_0=0,\ \mathcal A_1=3,\ \mathcal A_2=5,
\qquad
\mathcal B_0=0,\ \mathcal B_1=1,\ \mathcal B_2=2,
\]
and the same odd recurrence. At an even index, the indicated integer subtraction is converted back to a natural number by taking its nonnegative natural value.

We prove by strong induction on \(n\) that
\[
 \mathcal A_n=A_n,\qquad \mathcal B_n=B_n.                    \tag{30}
\]
The cases \(n=0,1,2\) are the initial values. At an odd index, substitution of the induction hypotheses into (1) immediately gives (30). At an even index, substitution into (2) identifies the integer expression used in the natural recurrence with \(A_n\), respectively \(B_n\). By (9), \(A_n\ge0\), and by (8), \(B_n\ge1\); thus converting those integer expressions to natural numbers does not truncate anything and returns exactly \(A_n\) and \(B_n\). This completes the induction.

Consequently the fractions formed from the OEIS numerator sequence A340737 and its corresponding denominator sequence A340738 are exactly \(A_n/B_n\). Their convergence to \(e\) now follows from (29).
